The '''52nd New Zealand Parliament''' was a meeting of the legislature in [[New Zealand]], which opened on 7 November 2017 following the [[2017 New Zealand general election|2017 general election]] and dissolved on 6 September 2020. The [[New Zealand Parliament]] comprises the Sovereign (represented by the [[Governor-General of New Zealand|governor-general]]) and the [[New Zealand House of Representatives|House of Representatives]], which consists of 120 members.<ref>{{cite web|title=Our system of government|url=http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/|publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)]]|access-date=24 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000229094103/http://electionresults.govt.nz/|archive-date=29 February 2000|url-status=live}}</ref>

The 52nd Parliament was elected using a [[mixed-member proportional representation]] (MMP) voting system. [[Member of parliament|Members of Parliament]] (MPs) represent 71 geographical electorates: 16 in the [[South Island]], 48 in the [[North Island]] and 7 [[Māori electorates]]. The remaining members were elected from [[Party lists in the 2017 New Zealand general election|party lists]] using the [[Webster/Sainte-Laguë method|Sainte-Laguë method]] to achieve proportionality. The number of geographical electorates was increased by one at the [[2014 New Zealand general election|2014 election]], to account for the [[North Island]]'s higher population growth.<ref name="electorate numbers and boundaries">{{cite web|title=Reviewing electorate numbers and boundaries |url=http://www.elections.org.nz/elections/electorates/reviewing-electorates.html |publisher=Elections New Zealand |access-date=6 January 2012 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20111109013802/http://www.elections.org.nz/elections/electorates/reviewing-electorates.html |archivedate=9 November 2011 |df=dmy }}</ref>

== Background ==
===2017 general election===
{{main|2017 New Zealand general election}}
The 2017 general election was held on Saturday, 23 September 2017. Voters elected 120 members to the House of Representatives, with 71 [[New Zealand electorates|electorate]] members and 49 [[Party lists in the 2017 New Zealand general election|list]] members. Official results indicated that the [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]] had won a plurality, winning 56 seats; down from 60 in 2014. The [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour Party]] won 46 seats, up from 32 at the last election. Their partner, the [[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Green Party]] won 8 seats, down from 14. [[New Zealand First]] won 9 seats, down from 11. [[ACT New Zealand|ACT]] won the electorate of [[Epsom (New Zealand electorate)|Epsom]], and enough party votes to avoid an overhang, but failed to win any more party votes to entitle it to more seats.<ref name="2017 general election results">{{cite web|title=2017 General Election – Official Result|url=http://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/|publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|New Zealand Electoral Commission]]|access-date=6 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180614123911/http://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/|archive-date=14 June 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Formation ===
Since neither the National–ACT or Labour–Green blocs managed to reach the necessary majority to form a government, New Zealand First was left in the position of kingmaker. Negotiations between New Zealand First and each of National and Labour continued over the next four weeks. On 19 October, Winston Peters announced he was forming a coalition agreement with Labour, with the Greens in a confidence-and-supply agreement. The Greens' support, plus the coalition, resulting in 63 seats to National's 56 – enough to ensure that Ardern maintained the confidence of the House.<ref name="Newshub"/><ref name="Newshub1"/> On 26 October 2017, Jacinda Ardern was sworn in as prime minister by Governor-General [[Patsy Reddy|Dame Patsy Reddy]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hurley |first1=Emma |title=As it happened: Jacinda Ardern sworn in as Prime Minister |url=https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2017/10/live-updates-jacinda-ardern-to-be-sworn-in-as-prime-minister.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171026022841/http://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2017/10/live-updates-jacinda-ardern-to-be-sworn-in-as-prime-minister.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=26 October 2017 |access-date=25 October 2020 |work=[[Newshub]] |date=26 October 2017 |language=en}}</ref>

== Parliamentary term ==

[[Jacinda Ardern]], as [[Leader of the New Zealand Labour Party|Leader of the Labour Party]], serves as [[Prime Minister of New Zealand|Prime Minister]]. [[Winston Peters]], as [[New Zealand First#Office-holders|Leader of New Zealand First]], serves as [[Deputy Prime Minister of New Zealand|Deputy Prime Minister]] and [[Minister of Foreign Affairs (New Zealand)|Minister of Foreign Affairs]]. Prime Minister Ardern appointed [[Grant Robertson]] as [[Minister of Finance (New Zealand)|Minister of Finance]], [[Ron Mark]] as [[Minister of Defence (New Zealand)|Minister of Defence]], [[Kelvin Davis (politician)|Kelvin Davis]] as [[Minister of Corrections (New Zealand)|Minister of Corrections]], [[David Parker (New Zealand politician)|David Parker]] as [[Attorney General (New Zealand)|Attorney General]], [[Andrew Little (New Zealand politician)|Andrew Little]] as [[Minister of Justice (New Zealand)|Minister of Justice]], [[David Clark (New Zealand politician)|Dr David Clark]] as [[Minister of Health (New Zealand)|Minister of Health]], and [[Chris Hipkins]] as [[Minister of Education (New Zealand)|Minister of Education]] and [[Leader of the House (New Zealand)|Leader of the House]].

For a period of six weeks beginning 21 June 2018, [[Winston Peters]] served as [[Acting Prime Minister]] of [[Prime Minister of New Zealand|New Zealand]], while Prime Minister [[Jacinda Ardern]] took maternity leave. Ardern was only the second [[head of government]] to give birth while in office, after [[Benazir Bhutto]], who gave birth while serving as [[Prime Minister of Pakistan]].

=== Major legislation ===
On 31 October 2017, Prime Minister [[Jacinda Ardern]] announced that for their first bill, the government would amend the Overseas Investment Act 2005 to categorise existing residential properties as "sensitive", restricting its sale to citizens and permanent residents only.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Hickey|first1=Bernard|last2=Sachdeva|first2=Sam|title=Labour's first act is to ban foreign buyers|url=https://www.newsroom.co.nz/2017/10/31/57280/labours-first-act-is-to-ban-foreign-buyers|access-date=2 November 2017|website=Newsroom.co.nz|date=31 October 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171031092757/https://www.newsroom.co.nz/2017/10/31/57280/labours-first-act-is-to-ban-foreign-buyers|archive-date=31 October 2017|url-status=live}}</ref> The [[Overseas Investment Amendment Act 2018]] was introduced on 14 December 2017 and received royal assent on 22 August 2018.<ref>{{cite web |title=Overseas Investment Amendment Bill - New Zealand Parliament |url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/BILL_75755/overseas-investment-amendment-bill |website=Parliament.nz |access-date=6 September 2020}}</ref>

On 8 November 2017, the Parental Leave and Employment Protection Amendment Bill was introduced and received royal assent on 4 December 2017. It extends paid parental leave to 22 weeks starting from 1 July 2018 and 26 weeks from 1 July 2020.<ref>{{cite web |title=Parental Leave and Employment Protection Amendment Bill - New Zealand Parliament |url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/BILL_75143/parental-leave-and-employment-protection-amendment-bill |website=Parliament.nz |access-date=6 September 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Cheng |first1=Derek |title=Bill extending paid parental leave to 26 weeks passes final reading in Parliament |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11950629 |access-date=6 September 2020 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=30 November 2017}}</ref>

On 4 December 2017, royal assent was given to the [[Healthy Homes Guarantee Act 2017|Healthy Homes Guarantee Bill]], which was introduced on 15 October 2015 during the previous Parliament. It ensures every rental house in the country meets standards of heating and insulation.<ref>{{cite web |title=Healthy Homes Guarantee Bill (No 2) - New Zealand Parliament |url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/00DBHOH_BILL66216_1/healthy-homes-guarantee-bill-no-2 |website=Parliament.nz |access-date=6 September 2020}}</ref>

On 22 December 2017, the [[Misuse of Drugs (Medicinal Cannabis) Amendment Bill]] was introduced, receiving royal assent on 17 December 2018. The act amends the [[Misuse of Drugs Act 1975]] to allow terminally ill patients to use cannabis, provide a regulatory body to set standards for cannabis products, and declassify [[cannabidiol]] as a controlled substance.<ref>{{cite web |title=Misuse of Drugs (Medicinal Cannabis) Amendment Bill - New Zealand Parliament |url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/BILL_75877/misuse-of-drugs-medicinal-cannabis-amendment-bill |website=Parliament.nz |access-date=6 September 2020}}</ref>

On 11 April 2019, royal assent was given to the [[Arms (Prohibited Firearms, Magazines, and Parts) Amendment Act 2019]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Arms (Prohibited Firearms, Magazines, and Parts) Amendment Bill - New Zealand Parliament|url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/BILL_86423/arms-prohibited-firearms-magazines-and-parts-amendment|access-date=2020-08-16|website=www.parliament.nz}}</ref> It amended the [[Arms Act 1983]] to ban semi-automatic firearms, magazines, and parts that can be used to assemble prohibited firearms.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Arms (Prohibited Firearms, Magazines, and Parts) Amendment Act 2019 No 12, Public Act Contents – New Zealand Legislation|url=http://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2019/0012/latest/LMS181180.html|access-date=2020-08-16|website=www.legislation.govt.nz}}</ref>

On 8 May 2019, the [[Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Bill]] was introduced, receiving royal assent on 13 November 2019. It provides a framework for developing [[Climate change in New Zealand|climate change policies]] in support of the [[Paris Agreement]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Bill - New Zealand Parliament |url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/BILL_87861/climate-change-response-zero-carbon-amendment-bill |website=Parliament.nz |access-date=6 September 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Young |first1=Audrey |title=Zero Carbon Bill passes with almost unanimous support in Parliament |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12283372 |access-date=6 September 2019 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=7 November 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191108191843/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12283372 |archive-date=8 November 2019 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

On 23 March 2020, the [[Abortion Legislation Act 2020|Abortion Legislation Act]] received royal assent, decriminalising abortion. Under the act, women can seek an abortion without restrictions within the first 20 weeks of their pregnancy.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Abortion Legislation Act 2020 No 6, Public Act Contents – New Zealand Legislation|url=http://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2020/0006/latest/LMS237550.html|access-date=2020-08-16|website=www.legislation.govt.nz}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-03-18|title=Abortion Legislation Bill passes third and final reading in Parliament|url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/412087/abortion-legislation-bill-passes-third-and-final-reading-in-parliament|access-date=2020-08-16|website=[[RNZ]] }}</ref>

On 12 May 2020, the [[COVID-19 Public Health Response Bill]] was introduced and speedily passed, receiving royal assent the day after. The bill establishes standalone legislation that provides a legal framework for responding to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in New Zealand]] for a period of up to 2 years.<ref>{{cite web |title=COVID-19 Public Health Response Bill - New Zealand Parliament |url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/BILL_97739/covid-19-public-health-response-bill |website=Parliament.nz |access-date=6 September 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Sadler |first1=Rachel |title=COVID-19 Public Health Response Bill passes in Parliament |url=https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2020/05/covid-19-public-health-response-bill-passes-in-parliament.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200528043729/https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2020/05/covid-19-public-health-response-bill-passes-in-parliament.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=28 May 2020 |access-date=6 September 2020 |work=[[Newshub]] |date=13 May 2020}}</ref>

=== Dissolution ===

Under section 17 of the [[Constitution Act 1986]], Parliament must dissolve a maximum of "3 years from the day fixed for the return of the [[Writ of election|writs]] issued for the last preceding general election of members of the House of Representatives, and no longer."<ref>{{cite web |title=Constitution Act 1986 No 114 (as at 17 May 2005), Public Act 17 Term of Parliament – New Zealand Legislation |url=http://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1986/0114/latest/DLM94241.html |website=New Zealand Legislation |publisher=New Zealand Government |access-date=15 September 2020 |date=1 July 1994}}</ref> The writ for the [[2017 New Zealand general election|2017 election]] was issued on 23 August 2017 and returned on 12 October 2017, meaning that the 52nd Parliament would have to dissolve on or before 12 October 2020.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.elections.org.nz/events/2017-general-election/2017-general-election-timetable |title= 2017 General Election timetable |publisher=Electoral Commission |access-date= 3 May 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170501201242/http://www.elections.org.nz/events/2017-general-election/2017-general-election-timetable |archive-date= 1 May 2017 |url-status= dead }}</ref>

This Parliament had its last scheduled sitting on 6 August 2020<ref name="original final day">{{cite news |last1=Cooke |first1=Henry |title=The last day of the coalition: Parliament wraps up with brutal jokes and moments of gratitude |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300076180/the-last-day-of-the-coalition-parliament-wraps-up-with-brutal-jokes-and-moments-of-gratitude |access-date=6 August 2020 |work=Stuff |date=6 August 2020}}</ref> and was originally set to be dissolved on 12 August.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Young |first1=Audrey |title=Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern
